schools.summary: Gill: since God appoints all things and performs them in their season, the times of executing his purposes cannot be hidden from him; the Vulgate flattens the clause to 'times are not hidden from the Almighty.'

Henry builds the doctrine of omniscience — past times not hidden from God's judgment, present from his providence, future from his prescience — yet those who know him do not see his day; the deferral is a mystery that exercises faith and prayer.

Clarke follows Good's 'doomsdays kept by the Almighty, that offenders may eye their periods'; Wesley reads 'times' as the fittest seasons for punishing the wicked, which if fixed would not be hidden from good men.
Ellicott: even those who love God are as perplexed about his government as those who know him not; the AV's second negative is better read 'see not' than 'not see.'

themes: times not hidden from the Almighty

schools.summary: Gill: removing the landmarks was forbidden as an accursed thing and known evil by the light of nature before the law; the heathen had their Jupiter Terminalis and Numa's death-penalty; some render 'they touch the landmarks.'
Henry reads it as disseizing neighbours of their inherited estate under pretence the marks were misplaced (Deut. 19:14; 27:17); forging deeds is now the equivalent crime.

Keil and Delitzsch render 'they steal flocks and shepherd them,' grazing the stolen as their own, and parse 'the times' with a genitive as the point when a man's fate is decided; Ellicott notes the Mosaic prohibition and reads 'feed them' (pasture the stolen flocks).
Clarke: Good takes the verb from a root 'to rend,' while the Septuagint read 'shepherd,' picturing the robbers 'carrying off both the flock and the shepherd.'
Gill: the fatherless with but a single ass, the more cruel to drive away because it is all he has.
Ellicott presses the singleness of ass and ox, catches a glimpse of an oppressed servile race, and notes the movement from the oppression of the country to that of the city (v.12).
Henry: God has made it a title of his honour to be Father of the fatherless and judge of the widows, and reckons their oppressors his enemies.
Wesley: to take the widow's ox for a pledge is contrary to God's law, written in the heart and in Exod. 22:26-27.

themes: the widow's ox for a pledge
God the Father of the fatherless

schools.summary: Gill: 'turn the needy out of the way' morally (from righteousness), civilly (from livelihood), or literally — the poor forced aside in fear.
Henry: the poor misled, bantered, turned from relief, threatened as vagabonds, and forced to abscond and hide themselves together.
Clarke: they oblige the poor to circuitous routes, the shutting-up of ancient rights-of-way; Wesley: the needy driven from the tyrants' path, hiding for fear of further injuries.

outliers.note: Illustrates the shutting-up of ancient rights-of-way with the tale of a poor cobbler who went to law against a nobleman and won, 'because I did not like to leave the world worse than I found it.'

themes: turning the needy out of the way

schools.summary: Gill keeps both readings open — the poor driven to forage like wild asses, or the wicked likened to the untamed ass, the wild Arabs living by plunder.
Clarke leans to a lawless roaming band, the Bedouins driven to the deserts by oppression; Wesley takes the wild asses as the lawless, greedy oppressors going forth to spoil.
Henry reads them plainly as robbers, of Ishmael's stamp (Gen. 16:12), for whom stealing is a trade they rise betimes to ply.

debates.question: Are the 'wild asses in the desert' the predatory wicked, or the oppressed poor driven to forage?

sides.position: the predatory wicked — marauding Arabs and robbers ranging after prey (of Ishmael's stamp)
the oppressed poor, driven to forage in the desert like wild creatures (a reading Gill keeps open beside the robber-reading)

themes: who is the subject — wicked or poor

schools.summary: Gill: the wicked reap the poor's standing corn openly, and some ancient versions read 'which is not their own.'
Clarke: the marauding hordes carry off the harvest into the wilderness (Chaldee 'a field not their own'); Wesley: they rob promiscuously, even the vintage of men as wicked as themselves.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take the corn and vintage as the rich tyrant's own, reaped and gathered by hands he leaves unfed.

debates.question: Whose is the 'vintage of the wicked' the robbers gather?

sides.position: the crop of another wicked man — the spoiler himself spoiled
the tyrant's own harvest, gathered by the labourers he leaves hungry

schools.summary: Gill: the naked are the plundered, stripped even of their bed-clothes, forced to lie all night uncovered.
Clarke: 'they spend the night naked' — a trait of the ill-clad wandering Arab; Wesley: the naked are those the oppressors have stripped of garments and coverings.
Henry: the robbers strip the poor of the clothes on their backs, and there are men truly guilty of the cruelties Eliphaz falsely charged on Job (ch. 22:6) who yet prosper.

debates.question: Are the 'naked' the oppressor's stripped victims or the wandering poor themselves?

sides.position: victims stripped by the strong of clothing and bed-covering
the ill-clothed wandering Arabs who spend the night naked

schools.summary: Gill: the ill-clothed are drenched by the mountain showers and the melting snow, wet as Nebuchadnezzar with the dew of heaven.

Clarke defends 'showers of the mountain' from his own sight of water-spouts broken on the peaks, the rock the only shelter to be trusted; Wesley: they are glad to find a cleft of the rock for some protection.
Henry: driven to embrace the rock, glad of a cave; Job argues more justly from an open course of wickedness than Eliphaz did from mere present trouble, the curse working invisibly.

themes: wet with the showers of the mountains

schools.summary: Gill weighs the motives — to starve, to sell into slavery, or to force the mother to early weaning; Broughton, 'of mischievousness they rob the fatherless.'
Clarke: children forcibly taken for bondage, and 'a pledge of the poor' of landlords seizing the labourer's cow, bed, or cart; Wesley: they will not allow the mother time to suckle her infant.

Henry: having made children fatherless they make them motherless too; Pharaoh and Herod plucked children to the sword (Hos. 9:13); to take the poor for a pledge is to rob the very hospital (Neh. 5:5).

themes: plucking the fatherless from the breast

schools.summary: Gill: the labourer, his raiment pledged or his wages withheld, is driven to go naked.
Clarke: they seize the family's cloth, or its wool and flax, and take the sheaf as soon as reaped to pay themselves their exorbitant rent.
Ellicott renders the expressive tautology — the poor 'go about naked' and 'an hungered carry the sheaves'; Keil and Delitzsch read the deliberate pairing of want with the harvest borne for another.
Henry: the masters forget they have a Master in heaven; to keep the sheaf-bearer hungry is worse than muzzling the ox that treads out the corn (Deut. 25:4).

themes: the sheaf taken from the hungry

schools.summary: Gill: the labourers press the oil among the olive-rows of their masters, at noon in the heat, and are given nothing to quench their thirst.
Clarke: reduced to vassals treading wine-presses of a produce they may not taste; Wesley: the oil made for the oppressors' use, thirst suffered because they may not drink the wine.
Henry: the kept-back hire of the labourers cries out (James 5:4); the masters grudge even the meat and drink that would keep them at their task.
Gill: the oppression is now done openly in the cities, where the courts of justice sit, yet in defiance of law and justice.
Henry: the city merchants are as cruel to their poor debtors as the country landlords to their tenants, and the oppressed cry out like wounded men.
Clarke brings the misery indoors from his own visit to a wretched London district and offers three renderings of the last clause; Wesley: 'yet God doth not punish them.'
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take 'God layeth not folly to them' of the oppressors, whom he charges with no folly and calls to no swift reckoning.

debates.question: What does 'yet God layeth not folly to them' mean?

sides.position: God charges the oppressors with no folly — sends no swift reckoning (their impunity)
God does not impute the calamity to the victims' folly; or (Vulgate) will not leave it unpunished; or does not attend their prayers

outliers.note: Illustrates the city's oppression from his own visit to a poor London district, where he found the dwellings crowded with the sick and the dead, sixty souls under one roof, and traces the misery to ruthless landlords and the ruin of unnecessary wars.

themes: men groan from out of the city
the soul of the wounded crieth out
God layeth not folly to them
oppression in defiance of the courts

schools.summary: Gill: the light of nature, or of the law (Targum), or God himself who is light and in whom is no darkness — every sin a rebellion against him.
Wesley: the light of reason, conscience, and revelation, which they neither approve nor love; Clarke: tyrants in grain who will not learn their duty and, if reformed, relapse.
Henry holds both senses — sinning against the light of conscience, and choosing the literal night for wickedness (works of darkness, John 3:20; ch. 34:22).
Keil and Delitzsch mark a new class whose character is that they shun the light; Ellicott finds the phrase remarkable, seeming to anticipate St John's teaching (John 1:9).

debates.question: Is 'the light' they rebel against moral or physical?

sides.position: the moral light — of nature, conscience, law, and revelation
both moral and physical — sinning against conscience and choosing the literal night

schools.summary: Gill: the murderer rises before sunrise to meet the early traveller and the poor labourer on the road.
Keil and Delitzsch render him a highwayman by day and a thief by night; Ellicott notes the order murder-adultery-theft follows the Decalogue, suggesting acquaintance with it.
Clarke (with Good) refers 'poor and needy' to the murderer himself, driven by poverty to the highway; Wesley: where he finds no booty he exercises his cruelty.
Henry: he kills poor travellers for a little, and at last for killing's sake, thirsting more for blood than for booty.

debates.question: Do 'the poor and needy' name the murderer's victim or the murderer himself?

sides.position: the victim — the humble traveller slain for the little he carries
the murderer — a man driven by poverty to rob and kill

themes: the murderer rising with the light
by day a highwayman, by night a thief
the Decalogue order of the crimes

schools.summary: Gill: the adulterer waits for the evening twilight to have the whole night, the eye singled out as the very inlet of the sin (2 Pet. 2:14).
Clarke: he makes his assignation, waits for the dusk, goes forth muffled, and dreads the dawn lest he be recognized and called to a sanguinary reckoning.
Henry: adultery hides for shame and for fear of the husband's jealousy (Prov. 6:34-35; 7:9); great pains taken to conceal what ends in death.
Gill: not the adulterers but the housebreakers, who mark houses full of goods by day and dig through walls and doors by night.
Wesley: the subject is the robber, the adulterer having been brought in beside him, now returned to his housebreaking.

Ellicott holds both — 'marked in the daytime' or 'seal themselves up by day' (the eastern access to the harem in female attire) — and notes 'they know not the light' differs from v.13; Keil and Delitzsch read a band of thieves who shut themselves up by day.
Henry: they dig through when the good man of the house lies exposed asleep (Luke 12:39); the law counts burglary a felony without benefit of clergy.

debates.question: Is the one who digs through houses the thief and burglar or the adulterer?

sides.position: the thief and housebreaker
the adulterer, or the two not always distinct

themes: digging through houses in the dark
marked by day or self-sealed by day

schools.summary: Gill: the morning is as hateful to them as the thickest darkness to others; better rendered 'alike' than 'even' — to all of them it wears the face of death.
Wesley: to them the morning is terrible and hateful.
Keil and Delitzsch: the depth of night is to them as the dawn of morning — natures so inverted that light and dark have changed places.
Henry: the daylight is a terror; they curse the sun because it discovers them and stand in the terrors of the shadow of death — a present, secret judgment.

themes: the morning as the shadow of death

schools.summary: Gill records the sea-robber reading but doubts such existed so early, and notes Schultens's guess of Sodomites.
Henry gives both the pirate reading (after bishop Patrick) and the swift escape of the light-hating sinner to a cursed, desolate portion.

Ellicott reads not a comparison but a swift escape over the waters, the wicked choosing lone paths; Keil and Delitzsch make the point the swift disappearing of a light thing on the current (ch. 9:26).
Clarke keeps 'light is he on the face of the waters,' the vintage failing; Wesley turns it to the wicked's transitory passing-away with all his glory.

debates.question: Does v.18 describe a new class of sea-robbers, the swift escape of the criminal, or the wicked's transitory passing?

sides.position: a new class of pirates or sea-robbers (a reading doubted)
the swift escape of the light-hating criminal over the water
the transitory rushing-away of the wicked toward his grave

outliers.note: Records Schultens's proposal that the verse describes Sodomites, profuse in lust and heedless of the honest labour of the vineyard, though Gill himself doubts sea-robbers existed so early.

themes: the cursed portion in the earth
turning from the way of the vineyards

schools.summary: Gill: as drought and heat melt and dry the snow-water, easily and all at once, so are sinners snatched to the grave.
Clarke: the great snow-fed cisterns exhausted by heat; on 'sheol chatau' (two words) sheol means any deep pit, and he follows Good's 'they fall to their lowest depth.'

Keil and Delitzsch render 'so doth Sheol those who have sinned,' opening the account of the wicked's death; Ellicott: Job had called the sudden death of the wicked a blessing (ch. 21:13) beside his own lingering torture.

themes: so doth the grave the sinner
the ease of the wicked's death

schools.summary: Gill canvasses whose womb forgets him — the mother, the wife, a friend, the earth, or God himself, the word carrying the sense of mercy.

Clarke: rechem is mercy — 'mercy shall be unmindful of him'; the worm feeds sweetly; 'broken as a tree' a rotten tree, or Good's 'the shoot broken off'; Wesley: broken to pieces, a tree once felled that never grows again.
Ellicott: some read the verse as what ought to befall the wicked rather than what does — a wish for justice, not a report of it.

debates.question: Does v.20 describe the wicked's actual oblivion, or what by rights ought to befall him?

sides.position: the actual, easy oblivion into which the wicked sink, unavenged
what ought to be his doom — a wish for justice

schools.summary: Gill: he uses the barren wife ill for her childlessness, or consorts with the barren and with harlots and wastes his substance.

Clarke reads the verb 'he feedeth the barren' (Vulgate) — kind where she profits him, but doing no good to the widow; Wesley: barrenness a reproach, so to entreat her evilly is to afflict the afflicted.
Henry likens it to Peninnah vexing Hannah; the barren are helpless, wanting the arrows of the quiver (Ps. 127:5), and not to do good to the widow is to do her hurt.

debates.question: Does the verb mean the wicked man wrongs the barren, or feeds (is kind to) her?

sides.position: he evil-entreats the barren — taunts and afflicts her
he feeds the barren (kind where she profits him) but does no good to the widow

themes: doing no good to the widow

schools.summary: Gill: the oppressor draws even the mighty into his party or his net by superior force, so that none is sure of life before him.
Henry: he becomes the terror of the mighty, drawing them into a snare, his hand against every man (Gen. 16:12).
Clarke (with Calmet): the tyrant draws guards for his defence yet, amid them, is not sure of his life — the inward terror of a despot.

Ellicott keeps the tyrant drawing others by influence and example; Keil and Delitzsch turn the subject to God — 'He preserveth the mighty by his strength,' raising up the wicked man who despaired of life.

debates.question: Who is the subject, and what does the verse describe?

sides.position: the tyrant overpowering even the mighty, so none is safe under him
the tyrant amid his own guards, living in terror for his life
God preserving and reviving the wicked mighty by his strength

themes: drawing the mighty with his power

schools.summary: Gill: God gives the wicked to be in safety despite his wickedness, yet his eyes are upon his ways.
Wesley: God grants strange successes yet observes all their ways and will punish in due time; Clarke reads the suspicious tyrant watching his own guards lest they plot his destruction.

Ellicott allows both the tyrant granting tribute for his security and God giving the man safety, his eyes on them all; Keil and Delitzsch: God gives him rest and sustains him, his eyes over their ways.

debates.question: Whose watching eyes are 'upon their ways'?

sides.position: God's eyes — marking the ways of men he has for a season let alone
the tyrant's eyes — fixed in distrust on the guards he dare not trust

themes: God's gaze or the despot's suspicion

schools.summary: Gill: exalted only 'for a little while,' the height and the fall named almost in one breath — a sentence that comes near to Zophar's.
Clarke: God turns his hand and they are gone, mown like grass and cropped like corn — few tyrants die a natural death; Wesley: taken out of the way as all others, cut off in their maturity.
Keil and Delitzsch: 'exalted a little while, then no more... cut off as the top of the stalk' — the stress on the suddenness of the feared man's ceasing to be.

themes: brought low and cut off like corn

schools.summary: Gill: if it be not so — that the wicked prosper, escape, and die quietly — let it be disproved.
Clarke: Job repels the friends' doctrine by fact, defying them to show a flaw; the middle way they missed — the wicked miserable in soul, the righteous happy in God.
Henry: let them prove his discourse false or beside the point; those who speak the words of truth need not fear a fair test.
Ellicott: Job also has his facts, as ready and incontrovertible as the friends', and yet irreconcilable with theirs.

themes: who will make me a liar
